opus-5.5.text:
Well, I should say up front that I'm not on the Seedance team, so I can only speak from the outside and from what I've seen working on visual generation and representation learning. But I think the general lesson applies to everyone building these video models.

"A lot of data" is almost the default now. Everyone can crawl huge amounts of video. The difference is in what you do with it. Raw internet video is extremely messy: there are scene cuts every few seconds, watermarks, subtitles, static slideshows, screen recordings, low frame rates, bad compression. If you feed all of that into a model naively, it learns those artifacts as faithfully as it learns real motion and physics. So the first part is really curation: splitting clips at the right boundaries, filtering for motion quality and aesthetics, removing duplicates, and balancing the distribution so the model isn't dominated by a few types of content.

The second part, which I think people underestimate, is captioning. For a text-to-video model, the caption *is* the supervision signal. If your captions just say "a man walking," the model never learns camera movement, lighting, the sequence of actions, or how multiple shots relate to each other. Teams that do well invest heavily in dense, structured, temporally aware descriptions, often using strong vision-language models in the loop, and then they iterate on that pipeline almost like a product of its own.

And third, there's a feedback loop between data and model. You train, you look at the failure cases, maybe hands look wrong, or multi-shot transitions are incoherent, and you go back and reshape the data mixture to target those. That's less like "collecting data" and more like engineering a curriculum.

So my view is that data is no longer a static resource you pile up. It's a system you design. In some sense, the data pipeline encodes a lot of the team's understanding of what good video looks like, and that taste and judgment is much harder to copy than the architecture.

r001.rationale: It describes captions as the text-to-video supervision signal and says they should capture the video’s actions, camera movement, lighting, and shot relationships, which communicates aligning video data with language prompts.

r002.rationale: It does not say that completing data preparation makes later work simpler.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the thing people underestimate about video is that "a lot of data" and "a lot of usable data" are almost different objects. For language, the web gives you text that is already roughly in the form you want to learn from. For video, raw footage is mostly noise relative to what the model actually needs: long static shots, shaky handheld clips, hard cuts every two seconds, watermarks, burned-in subtitles, duplicates, and clips where nothing happens that teaches the model anything about motion or physics.

So the first thing the data pipeline has to do is decompose. You don't train on a ten-minute video; you train on shots. That means scene detection, cutting at boundaries, and then deciding which segments are worth keeping. And the filtering is not just aesthetic. You care about motion quality, camera stability, whether the clip is temporally coherent, whether the content is diverse enough that the model isn't just memorizing one style of stock footage.

The second thing, and I think this is where the real leverage is, is captioning. A video without a good description is nearly useless for a text-conditioned generator. The model learns the mapping from language to visual dynamics, so if your captions are "a man in a room," you've thrown away most of the signal. You need dense captions that describe the subject, the action, the camera movement, the lighting, the temporal structure, what changes over the clip. And that requires a strong vision-language model in the loop, which means the data pipeline is itself a model-building problem. The quality of your captioner becomes a ceiling on the quality of your generator.

Then there's balancing. If you just scrape, your distribution is wildly skewed toward whatever is popular online. You end up with too many talking heads and not enough of the long tail: unusual camera moves, multi-subject interactions, rare physical events. Part of data preparation is actively reshaping that distribution, and sometimes synthesizing or augmenting to fill the gaps.

So my view is that the scaling law story is real, but the x-axis is not "hours of video." It's something closer to "hours of well-segmented, well-captioned, well-balanced video," and getting from the first to the second is most of the work. The teams that look like they just have more data usually have a much better pipeline.

r001.rationale: The response says captions must describe the video’s content and dynamics because the model learns a mapping from language to visual dynamics, communicating alignment between video data and language prompts.

r002.rationale: The response says data preparation is most of the work and affects generator quality, but does not state that completing it makes subsequent work much simpler.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between having a lot of data and having data that gives the model a useful learning signal. For video, that’s especially complicated. A clip can look beautiful frame by frame but contain very little motion, or it can have interesting motion but poor visual quality. So simply counting hours doesn’t tell you how useful the dataset is.

Data preparation means deciding what to keep, how to segment it, and how to describe what actually happens. The captions need to capture actions, temporal relationships, and camera movement, rather than just list the objects in a scene. You also need a balanced distribution, so the model sees different kinds of subjects and motion instead of repeatedly learning the most common patterns.

I wouldn’t claim to know Seedance’s exact internal pipeline, but that’s why I’d view this as a substantial engineering and research problem. The value comes from turning raw video into something the model can learn from reliably, not just accumulating more of it.

r001.rationale: The response says captions should describe actions, timing, and camera movement, but it does not clearly state that preparation calibrates alignment between video data and language prompts.

r002.rationale: The response calls data preparation a substantial engineering and research problem, but does not say that completing it makes subsequent work simpler.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that having a lot of data and having useful training data are two different things. For video, you need to consider visual quality, motion, temporal consistency, and whether the text actually describes what happens. A clip can look beautiful but provide a weak learning signal if its caption misses the action or the sequence of events.

So data preparation is really about turning raw videos into examples the model can learn from: selecting, filtering, organizing, and describing them. You also need a balanced distribution, so the model sees different kinds of scenes and movement. Simply adding more data can amplify noise or repetition. The important question is what each example teaches the model.

r001.rationale: It says the text should accurately describe what happens in each video, including its actions and sequence of events, communicating alignment between video data and language.

r002.rationale: It describes data preparation and why it matters, but does not say that completing it makes subsequent work simpler.
